headline: Uber positions itself as a mission-driven, inclusive tech company reshaping transportation through talent and diversity.
identity: Uber has consistently valued impact (moving people and improving cities), meritocracy (best ideas win), and inclusion—though the language around these has shifted markedly. Impact and meritocracy remained steady from 2011–2019, but DEI language surged from 2017–2019 (peaking at 0.63 inclusion score in 2018), then collapsed by 2024 (dropping to 0.32), when the careers copy pivoted almost entirely to accessibility features and disability accommodation rather than broad diversity and belonging rhetoric.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are driven by hard problems and measurable impact on real people's lives, thrive in a fast-moving environment where talent and ideas are valued over hierarchy, and—until 2019—were drawn to explicit commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion. By 2024, the company's language suggests a fit for those focused on accessibility and serving people with disabilities, though the broader DEI messaging has largely receded.

sections.heading: The Early Mission: Talent, Challenge, and Impact (2011–2015)
sections.body: From 2011 through 2015, Uber's careers copy centered on three pillars: attracting "extremely talented people," emphasizing that "the best idea always wins," and framing work as having real-world impact—"your contributions will not just move bits, but move actual people." The language was lean and performance-focused. Altruism scores were negative (zscore –1.3 in 2011, –0.6 by 2015), meaning the company leaned less on social good than peers; instead, it emphasized the challenge itself and the importance of individual talent. Meritocracy and performance language remained strong throughout (zscore 0.4–0.3), with quotes like "At Uber, the best idea always wins" and "We empower our teams to find creative solutions to difficult problems" appearing consistently. Inclusion and DEI language were absent or minimal—the careers pages made no explicit mention of diversity, women, LGBTQ+ issues, or belonging.

sections.heading: The Pivot to Altruism and Inclusion (2016–2019)
sections.body: Starting in 2016, Uber's self-description shifted. Altruism language jumped sharply (zscore 0.67 in 2016, peaking at 1.51 in 2018–2019), with new framing around "improving local economies," "making roads safer," and "bringing opportunities to millions." More significantly, DEI language exploded. In 2017, the company introduced "We want to create a workplace that is inclusive and reflects the diversity of the cities we serve" and began publishing diversity reports. By 2018–2019, DEI became central: inclusion scores hit 0.63–0.68, with explicit mentions of "women and underrepresented populations," "pay equity," "LGBTQ+ community," "bias mitigation," and "authentic self." The company stated "We have the audacious goal of being the most inclusive workplace in the world" and detailed structural changes—diversity sourcing teams, structured interviews, anti-bias training. Wellbeing language also rose (zscore 1.3 in 2018), emphasizing that diversity and inclusion made the company "better for our employees and our customers."

sections.heading: The Retreat from DEI (2020–2024)
sections.body: After 2019, the signal weakens sharply. Data from 2020–2023 is sparse (thin=true), but by 2024, the shift is unmistakable. DEI language collapsed: inclusion scores fell from 0.63 to 0.32, with only 29% of chunks containing any inclusion-related language (down from 96% in 2019). The explicit demographic and structural-process language—"women," "underrepresented," "diversity sourcing," "bias"—largely vanished. Instead, 2024's careers copy pivoted to accessibility and disability: "Our technology and the transportation provided by drivers has transformed mobility for many people with disabilities," "WAV (wheelchair-accessible vehicles)," "deaf or hard of hearing drivers," "service animals." Altruism remained moderate (zscore 0.49), but now framed around access for people with disabilities rather than broad economic opportunity or systemic inclusion. Performance and meritocracy language also declined (zscore –1.28 in 2024, the lowest on record), replaced by product-focused, accessibility-centered messaging. The company's self-description narrowed from "most inclusive workplace in the world" to a more technical, feature-driven narrative about serving specific populations.
